claim: The claustrum is thought to be one of the most highly interconnected forebrain structures.
source: The claustrum is thought to be one of the most highly interconnected forebrain structures, but its organizing principles have yet to be fully explored at the level of single neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the general understanding of the claustrum's connectivity, supported by established scientific knowledge and implied citations in the broader context.

claim: Neurons in the claustrum communicate with each other across efferent projection-defined modules which were differentially innervated by sensory and frontal cortical areas.
source: We found that neurons in the claustrum communicate with each other across efferent projection-defined modules which were differentially innervated by sensory and frontal cortical areas.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental data collected by the authors.

claim: Individual claustrum neurons were responsive to inputs from more than one cortical region in a cell-type and projection-specific manner, particularly between areas of frontal cortex.
source: Individual claustrum neurons were responsive to inputs from more than one cortical region in a cell-type and projection-specific manner, particularly between areas of frontal cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on experimental data from optogenetic mapping experiments.

claim: In vivo imaging of claustrum axons revealed responses to both unimodal and multimodal sensory stimuli.
source: In vivo imaging of claustrum axons revealed responses to both unimodal and multimodal sensory stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Chronic claustrum silencing specifically reduced animals' sensitivity to multimodal stimuli.
source: Finally, chronic claustrum silencing specifically reduced animals' sensitivity to multimodal stimuli.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on behavioral experiments with claustrum silencing.

claim: The claustrum has been implicated in sleep.
source: The claustrum (CLA) - defined by its dense connectivity with the cerebral cortex - has been implicated in a variety of the sensory and cognitive functions, including sleep (Narikiyo et al., 2020; Norimoto et al., 2020; Marriott et al., 2024)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The claustrum has been implicated in saliency detection.
source: The claustrum (CLA) - defined by its dense connectivity with the cerebral cortex - has been implicated in a variety of the sensory and cognitive functions, including sleep (Narikiyo et al., 2020; Norimoto et al., 2020; Marriott et al., 2024), saliency detection (Mathur, 2014; Remedios et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The claustrum has been implicated in multisensory integration.
source: The claustrum (CLA) - defined by its dense connectivity with the cerebral cortex - has been implicated in a variety of the sensory and cognitive functions, including sleep (Narikiyo et al., 2020; Norimoto et al., 2020; Marriott et al., 2024), saliency detection (Mathur, 2014; Remedios et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2019), multisensory integration (Crick and Koch, 2005; Smythies et al., 2012; Smythies et al., 2014; Vidyasagar and Levichkina, 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The claustrum has been implicated in task engagement.
source: The claustrum (CLA) - defined by its dense connectivity with the cerebral cortex - has been implicated in a variety of the sensory and cognitive functions, including sleep (Narikiyo et al., 2020; Norimoto et al., 2020; Marriott et al., 2024), saliency detection (Mathur, 2014; Remedios et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2019), multisensory integration (Crick and Koch, 2005; Smythies et al., 2012; Smythies et al., 2014; Vidyasagar and Levichkina, 2019), and task engagement (Atlan et al., 2021; Fodoulian et al., 2020; Jackson et al., 2018; Dillingham et al., 2017; Goll et al., 2015; Faig et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The claustrum is reciprocally connected with large swaths of cortex in a projection pattern that has been previously described as a 'crown of thorns'.
source: Lesion and anatomical studies point to a multifunctional role (Atilgan et al., 2022; Edelstein and Denaro, 2004; Patru and Reser, 2015), with CLA reciprocally connected with large swaths of cortex in a projection pattern that has been previously described as a 'crown of thorns' (Atlan et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2023; Zingg et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The claustrum preferentially projects to prefrontal and midline cortical regions.
source: Recent research has made it increasingly clear that this connectivity is not uniform, with CLA preferentially projecting to prefrontal and midline cortical regions (Wang et al., 2023; Zingg et al., 2014; Zingg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Claustrum projections appear to be organized into connectivity-defined modules within the CLA.
source: These projections appear to be organized into connectivity-defined modules within the CLA (Chia et al., 2020; Marriott et al., 2021; Gattass et al., 2014; Remedios et al., 2010), leading to functional selectivity (Atlan et al., 2021; Chevée et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Cortical projections to the CLA target efferent-defined modules and activate a dense network of feed-forward inhibition via local interneurons.
source: For example, cortical projections to the CLA target efferent-defined modules and activate a dense network of feed-forward inhibition via local interneurons (Chia et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2016; Ham and Augustine, 2022; LeVay and Sherk, 1981; Smith et al., 2012; Smith and Alloway, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Cell types in the CLA of mice are responsive to inputs from more than one cortical area.
source: Recently, it has been discovered that cell types in the CLA of mice are responsive to inputs from more than one cortical area (Qadir et al., 2022; Yuan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: CTB injection into the retrosplenial cortex labels CLA neurons specifically with no labeling of CLA-adjacent structures.
source: To label CLA neurons in the adult mouse, we used a retrograde tracing strategy by injecting fluorescently labeled cholera toxin subunit B (CTB) into the retrosplenial cortex (RSP), which receives input specifically from the CLA and no CLA-adjacent structures (Zingg et al., 2018; Marriott et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by the experimental design and cited references.

claim: Each CTB injection into different rostrocaudal locations of RSP labeled spatially overlapping populations of CLA neurons.
source: Confocal microscopy imaging of 100 μm-thick coronal sections revealed that each injection labeled spatially overlapping populations of CLA neurons, distinct from the surrounding, unlabeled tissue (Figure 1B, C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental imaging data.

claim: The caudal injection site in RSP reliably labeled the most CLA cells overall, especially in caudal regions of CLA.
source: A comparison between injection sites of CTB labeling in CLA across mice showed that the caudal injection site reliably labeled the most cells overall, especially in caudal regions of CLA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data comparing injection sites.

claim: CLARSP neurons could be found along the whole CLA length, irrespective of RSP injection location.
source: Further, this strategy consistently demonstrated that CLARSP neurons could be found along the whole CLA length, as defined by other sources (Franklin and Paxinos, 2008; Wang et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020; Grimstvedt et al., 2023), irrespective of RSP injection location.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data and comparison with anatomical references.

claim: The level of overlap between CLA neurons projecting to different regions of RSP varied depending on the injection site.
source: Moreover, the level of overlap between CLA neurons projecting to different regions of RSP varied depending on the injection site (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data.

claim: CLARSP neurons were aligned with the parvalbumin (PV) neuropil-rich CLA 'core' and a paucity of myelinated axons in the same region.
source: CLARSP neurons were aligned with the parvalbumin (PV) neuropil-rich CLA 'core' and a paucity of myelinated axons in the same region, as shown by myelin basic protein (MBP).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on immunohistochemistry data.

claim: The density of CLARSP neurons varied along the rostrocaudal axis with the highest number found around 1 mm rostral to bregma.
source: Analysis of thin (50 μm), sequential coronal sections demonstrated that the density of CLARSP neurons varied along the rostrocaudal axis (n=3 mice, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) with the highest number of CLARSP neurons found around 1 mm rostral to bregma (1070±261 cells/animal, 27±11 cells/section; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on cell counting data.

claim: Rostrally-located CLARSP neurons were found at low density showing a dispersed distribution.
source: The rostral and caudal poles of CLA differed in that rostrally-located CLARSP neurons were found at low density, that is showing a dispersed distribution, whereas neurons found 1 mm caudal to bregma were densely packed in a relatively small cross-section of tissue.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on anatomical analysis.

claim: Neurons found 1 mm caudal to bregma were densely packed in a relatively small cross-section of tissue.
source: The rostral and caudal poles of CLA differed in that rostrally-located CLARSP neurons were found at low density, that is showing a dispersed distribution, whereas neurons found 1 mm caudal to bregma were densely packed in a relatively small cross-section of tissue.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on anatomical analysis.

claim: Two excitatory cell subtypes (E1 and E2) were identified in the CLA based on intrinsic electrophysiological properties.
source: We identified several subtypes of both putative excitatory (total number of cells recovered: n=434) and inhibitory (n=106) neurons based on intrinsic electrophysiological properties (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings and analysis.

claim: Four inhibitory cell subtypes (HR, FS, LT, IR) were identified in the CLA based on intrinsic electrophysiological properties.
source: Interneurons, by contrast, were readily categorized into four groups (high rheobase [HR], fast-spiking [FS], low threshold [LT], irregular [IR]) using unsupervised methods alone (average inhibitory silhouette score = 0.853, k=4 clusters; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on electrophysiological recordings and unsupervised clustering analysis.

claim: E1 neurons show monophasic spike amplitude adaptation.
source: E1 and E2 neurons could be divided by spike amplitude adaptation normalized from the first action potential: E1 monophasically declined while E2 showed a biphasic pattern, initially declining sharply before recovering slightly (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on electrophysiological analysis.

claim: E2 neurons show a biphasic pattern of spike amplitude adaptation, initially declining sharply before recovering slightly.
source: E1 and E2 neurons could be divided by spike amplitude adaptation normalized from the first action potential: E1 monophasically declined while E2 showed a biphasic pattern, initially declining sharply before recovering slightly (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on electrophysiological analysis.

claim: E2 neurons have an afterdepolarization potential that leads to a bursting spike doublet at higher current injections.
source: E2 neurons could be further differentiated from E1 neurons by the presence of an afterdepolarization potential that led to a bursting spike doublet at higher current injections (ADP, 1.9±2.3 mV; Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on electrophysiological analysis.

claim: FS cells fire short half-width duration spikes at frequencies tested up to 200 Hz.
source: FS cells were found to fire short half-width duration spikes at frequencies tested up to 200 Hz, while LT cells had a low rheobase and high input resistance.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on electrophysiological analysis.

claim: LT cells have a low rheobase and high input resistance.
source: FS cells were found to fire short half-width duration spikes at frequencies tested up to 200 Hz, while LT cells had a low rheobase and high input resistance.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on electrophysiological analysis.

claim: HR cells have a large rheobase and low input resistance with a significant delay to spike at threshold.
source: Conversely, HR cells had a large rheobase and low input resistance with a significant delay to spike at threshold.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on electrophysiological analysis.

claim: HR interneurons are sparsely spiny with a dense dendritic arbor similar to that reported for neurogliaform cells.
source: Morphologically, HR interneurons were sparsely spiny (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) with a dense dendritic arbor similar to that reported for neurogliaform cells.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on morphological analysis and comparison with known cell types.

claim: IR cells fire irregularly and very infrequently compared to other types.
source: Finally, IR cells fired irregularly and very infrequently compared to other types.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on electrophysiological analysis.

claim: A small subset of putative interneurons was found to be CTB+, suggesting the presence of inhibitory projection neurons within the CLA.
source: Surprisingly, a small subset of putative interneurons was found to be CTB+ (some of which were co-labeled with tdTomato in Nkx2.1-Cre;Ai9 +animals; Figure 1—figure supplement 6), suggesting the presence of inhibitory projection neurons within the CLA.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on retrograde labeling and genetic labeling data.

claim: Inhibitory projection neurons represented 23% of putative inhibitory subtypes and 5% of total CLA neurons.
source: These cells, the majority of which were HR neurons, represented 23% of our putative inhibitory subtypes and 5% of total CLA neurons (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on cell counting data.

claim: GABAergic cells were captured using retrograde labeling approaches.
source: Further to this, we used immunohistochemistry to independently confirm that GABAergic cells were captured using retrograde labeling approaches (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on immunohistochemistry validation.

claim: The majority of E1 and E2 subtypes had spiny dendrites, consistent with them being excitatory neurons.
source: We reconstructed 134 recovered morphologies (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) and found the majority of E1 and E2 subtypes had spiny dendrites, consistent with them being excitatory neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on morphological reconstruction data.

claim: FS, HR, LT, and IR types were either aspiny or sparsely spiny in line with cortical GABAergic interneurons.
source: FS, HR, LT, and IR types were either aspiny or sparsely spiny in line with cortical GABAergic interneurons.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on morphological analysis and comparison with known cell types.

claim: No neuronal subtype was found to be exclusive to the CLARSP module.
source: Overall, our patch-clamp recorded neurons expand on previous knowledge of CLA neuron diversity Graf et al., 2020; Qadir et al., 2022, revealing a mix of excitatory and inhibitory neurons within this nucleus. No neuronal subtype was found to be exclusive to the CLARSP module, suggesting that efferent connectivity is not subtype specific.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on analysis of cell type distribution across projection targets.

claim: Efferent connectivity in the CLA is not subtype specific.
source: No neuronal subtype was found to be exclusive to the CLARSP module, suggesting that efferent connectivity is not subtype specific.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that no cell type is exclusive to CLARSP.

claim: Short-latency, putative monosynaptic EPSPs could be evoked in the majority (69.5%) of recorded CLA neurons by optogenetic stimulation of CLARSP axons.
source: We found that we could evoke short-latency, putative monosynaptic excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) in the majority (69.5%; n=32/46) of recorded CLA neurons, although only a small subset of these were CLARSP neurons (n=4/11 CTB + cells responsive; Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: Only a small subset of CLARSP neurons (n=4/11 CTB+ cells) were responsive to CLARSP optogenetic stimulation.
source: We found that we could evoke short-latency, putative monosynaptic excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) in the majority (69.5%; n=32/46) of recorded CLA neurons, although only a small subset of these were CLARSP neurons (n=4/11 CTB + cells responsive; Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: Both excitatory and inhibitory neuronal subtypes exhibited EPSPs in response to CLARSP optogenetic stimulation.
source: In addition, we found that both excitatory and inhibitory neuronal subtypes exhibited EPSPs in response to CLARSP optogenetic stimulation (Figure 2E, bottom right), although there were some differences between subtypes.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: E1 neurons (75.0%) were more likely to receive local CLARSP input than E2 neurons (59.1%).
source: Of the excitatory cell subtypes, E1 (75.0%) was more likely to receive local CLARSP input than E2 neurons (59.1%), despite the latter group being the predominant subtype in the CLA (Figure 2E, top).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: FS neurons (100%) exhibited the highest probability of receiving CLARSP input among inhibitory subtypes.
source: Among inhibitory subtypes, FS neurons (100%) exhibited the highest probability of receiving CLARSP input, while LT neurons (66.7%) received CLARSP input with probabilities comparable to that of excitatory types.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: LT neurons (66.7%) received CLARSP input with probabilities comparable to that of excitatory types.
source: Among inhibitory subtypes, FS neurons (100%) exhibited the highest probability of receiving CLARSP input, while LT neurons (66.7%) received CLARSP input with probabilities comparable to that of excitatory types.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: No statistically significant differences were found between cell types in the likelihood of responding to intraclaustral input.
source: Despite variability in these response probabilities, we found no statistically significant differences between cell types in the likelihood of responding to intraclaustral input (P>0.05, Fisher Exact test between all types, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study based on analysis of optogenetic stimulation data.

claim: The primary factor underpinning the organization of intraclaustral connectivity is projection target.
source: These data suggest – with implications for information transfer within the CLA – that the primary factor underpinning the organization of intraclaustral connectivity is projection target, that is CLA neurons that project to areas outside of RSP are more likely to receive local input from those that do (CLARSP).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data suggesting a principle of organization based on the experimental findings.

claim: CLA neurons that project to areas outside of RSP are more likely to receive local input from CLARSP neurons.
source: These data suggest – with implications for information transfer within the CLA – that the primary factor underpinning the organization of intraclaustral connectivity is projection target, that is CLA neurons that project to areas outside of RSP are more likely to receive local input from those that do (CLARSP).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on optogenetic stimulation experiments comparing CTB+ and CTB- neurons.

claim: Electrical stimulation of the rostral pole of the CLA resulted in a traveling wave of increased voltage that spread to caudal CLA over a period of 10–15ms.
source: Electrical stimulation of the rostral pole of the CLA resulted in a traveling wave of increased voltage that spread to caudal CLA over a period of 10–15ms.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on voltage-sensitive dye imaging experiments.

claim: Blocking glutamate receptors by bath application of DNQX and APV abolished voltage responses in the CLA, supporting a role for glutamatergic transmission within the rodent CLA.
source: Blocking glutamate receptors by bath application of DNQX and APV abolished these responses, supporting a role for glutamatergic transmission within and along the rodent CLA.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on pharmacological manipulation during voltage-sensitive dye imaging.

claim: Glutamatergic transmission in the CLA is bidirectional.
source: This transmission was bidirectional as electrical stimulation of caudal CLA elicited a wave of depolarization toward the rostral pole with similar temporal properties.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on voltage-sensitive dye imaging experiments.

claim: Cortical projections to CLA arrange into modules along the dorsoventral axis.
source: Much like CLA efferents (Marriott et al., 2021), we found that cortical projections to CLA arrange into modules along the dorsoventral axis, a similar finding to other studies (Atlan et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on anatomical tracing experiments and comparison with previous studies.

claim: ORB and ACAa projected to CLARSP both medially and laterally in addition to dorsally or ventrally.
source: Interestingly, certain cortices such as ORB and ACAa projected to CLARSP both medially and laterally in addition to dorsally or ventrally.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on anatomical tracing experiments.

claim: CLARSP neurons are more likely to respond to frontal cortical regions than non-CLARSP neurons.
source: Physiological investigations of cortical input revealed that CLARSP neurons are more likely to respond to frontal cortical regions than non-CLARSP neurons.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: CLA neurons, especially non-CLARSP neurons, were far more likely to respond to secondary visual cortex input in vitro than has been reported in primary sensory cortices.
source: Surprisingly, however, we found that CLA neurons, especially non-CLARSP neurons, were far more likely to respond to secondary visual cortex input in vitro, more so than has been reported in primary sensory cortices (Chia et al., 2020; White et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on optogenetic stimulation experiments and comparison with previous studies.

claim: Individual CLA neurons are frequently responsive to multiple different cortical inputs.
source: Our findings demonstrate that individual CLA neurons are frequently responsive to multiple different inputs.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on dual-color optogenetic experiments.

claim: Integration of cortical inputs was especially true for CLARSP when the cortices in question were both frontal.
source: This was especially true for CLARSP when the cortices in question were both frontal, while the balance of responsiveness shifted to non-CLARSP when other cortical areas were involved.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on dual-color optogenetic experiments.

claim: E2 and FS CLA cell types are highly integrative.
source: Specifically, we found the E2 and FS CLA cell types to be highly integrative, while other types were much less so.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on dual-color optogenetic experiments.

claim: E2 excitatory neurons were the most likely to project to RSP.
source: In addition, E2 excitatory neurons were the most likely to project to RSP.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on analysis of CTB labeling in different cell types.

claim: Integration of inputs to the CLA by E2 neurons may contribute to contextual processing in the RSP.
source: Given that RSP is strongly associated with contextual and spatial awareness (Trask et al., 2021), it is possible that integration of inputs to the CLA by E2 neurons contributes to contextual processing in the RSP and may explain our multimodal conditioning results when these neurons were silenced.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting the findings to known functions of RSP and behavioral results.

claim: Cell type identity, as defined by intrinsic electrophysiology and efferent projection target, influenced the likelihood that a neuron was dual-responsive to afferent input in the CLA.
source: Overall, cell type identity, as defined by intrinsic electrophysiology and efferent projection target, influenced the likelihood that a neuron was dual-responsive to afferent input in the CLA in these experiments.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the study based on dual-color optogenetic experiments.

claim: CLA axons innervate the cortical layers of ACA and RSP differently.
source: We found that CLA axons innervate the cortical layers of ACA and RSP differently, confirming and expanding on results from recent works (Jackson et al., 2018; McBride et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on in vitro optogenetic experiments and comparison with previous studies.

claim: ACA was innervated relatively evenly across layers and more so in deep layers than RSP for excitation and inhibition.
source: Overall, ACA was innervated relatively evenly across layers and more so in deep layers than RSP for excitation and inhibition.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on in vitro optogenetic experiments.

claim: A large proportion of responsive CLA axons were exclusively activated in trials where two or more stimuli were presented simultaneously.
source: A large proportion of responsive CLA axons were exclusively activated in trials where two or more stimuli were presented simultaneously.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claim: 47% of tested axons displayed significant calcium transients to at least one stimulus modality during passive presentation.
source: 47% of tested axons displayed significant calcium transients to at least one stimulus modality during passive presentation, and all modalities could evoke responses in at least some CLA axons (Figure 6D and E top left; Figure 6—figure supplement 2D, right).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claim: For unimodal stimulus presentations, somatosensory stimuli (whisker) were the most likely to elicit changes in fluorescence (18.8% of recorded axons).
source: For unimodal stimulus presentations, somatosensory stimuli (whisker) were the most likely to elicit changes in fluorescence, followed by light and then sound (18.8% of recorded axons responded to whisker, 12.1% to light, 10.9% to sound).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claim: The combination of all three stimuli resulted in the largest proportion of activated axons (20.7%).
source: The combination of all three stimuli resulted in the largest proportion of activated axons (20.7%), while the blank period was associated with the fewest responsive axons (9.8%, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claim: 85% of responsive axons were responsive to at least one or more multi-modal trial types.
source: 85% of responsive axons were responsive to at least one or more multi-modal trial types.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Of sensory-responsive axons, only 4% displayed unisensory response patterns, while 96% displayed multisensory response patterns.
source: Of sensory-responsive axons, only 4% of axons were found to display unisensory response patterns, while 96% displayed multisensory response patterns.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claim: 35% of stimulus-responsive CLA axons were exclusively responsive to multimodal trial types.
source: Interestingly, 35% of stimulus-responsive CLA axons were exclusively responsive to multimodal trial types, while 15% were exclusively responsive to unimodal trial types (Figure 6E, bottom).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claim: 15% of stimulus-responsive CLA axons were exclusively responsive to unimodal trial types.
source: Interestingly, 35% of stimulus-responsive CLA axons were exclusively responsive to multimodal trial types, while 15% were exclusively responsive to unimodal trial types (Figure 6E, bottom).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on in vivo calcium imaging experiments.

claim: The probability of observing a sensory-evoked response in a given field of view did not change over the course of experimentation.
source: With respect to the reliability of axonal responses to sensory stimulation, we found that the probability of observing a sensory-evoked response in a given field of view regardless of stimulus type did not change, on average, over the course of experimentation (Figure 6F, r=0.21, p=0.32).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on statistical analysis of in vivo calcium imaging data.

claim: Axonal response probability was significantly modulated between stimulus types.
source: However, axonal response probability was significantly modulated between stimulus types (Figure 6G, p=3.7e-9 Kruskal Wallis test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study based on in vivo calcium imaging data.

claim: Stimulus type was found to be a significant source of variation in the magnitude of axonal responses.
source: Similarly, stimulus type was found to be a significant source of variation in the magnitude of axonal responses (Figure 6H, p=6.4e-10 Kruskal Wallis test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study based on in vivo calcium imaging data.

claim: TetTox reduced the frequency and magnitude of light-evoked currents in downstream RSP cells, effectively silencing CLARSP output.
source: Patch-clamp recordings of RSP neurons revealed that TetTox reduced the frequency and magnitude of light-evoked currents in downstream cells, effectively silencing CLARSP output (p=0.0003, Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on in vitro validation experiments.

claim: Silencing CLARSP output did not significantly alter behavior in home cage recordings or tests for anxiety.
source: We found that silencing CLARSP output did not significantly alter the behavior of TetTox animals compared to the sham group.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on behavioral experiments.

claim: No differences were identified between CLA-silenced and sham groups in the reversal learning task across a number of metrics including response probability and latency.
source: We identified no differences between CLA-silenced and sham groups across a number of metrics including response probability and latency (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on behavioral experiments.

claim: CLARSP-silenced mice had significantly lower poke latencies across trial types and outcomes in the multimodal conditioning task.
source: First, we found that CLARSP-silenced mice had significantly lower poke latencies across trial types and outcomes (Figure 7H,I).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on behavioral experiments.

claim: CLARSP silencing specifically impaired animals' sensitivity to multimodal stimuli (p=0.001).
source: Second, a two-way ANOVA identified a significant interaction when comparing animals' sensitivity (the difference in the distributions of the hit rate and false alarm rate) to different trial types (F(2, 52)=5.53, p=0.006; Figure 7J). After correcting for multiple comparisons (Sidak), we found that CLARSP silencing specifically impaired animals' sensitivity to multimodal stimuli (p=0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study based on behavioral experiments.

claim: CLARSP silencing did not impact animals' responses to unimodal stimuli.
source: These results suggest that CLARSP silencing specifically reduced animals' sensitivity to multimodal stimuli without impacting their responses to unimodal stimuli.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on behavioral experiments.

claim: The integrative properties of the CLA may have functional relevance for detecting the coincidence or conjunction of two stimuli in the context of sensory-guided behavior.
source: This suggests that the integrative properties of the CLA described above may have functional relevance for detecting the coincidence or conjunction of two stimuli in the context of sensory-guided behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the anatomical and physiological findings to the behavioral results.
